taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes the English name Boreal Toad is sometimes used for this taxon (and older references use the genus Bufo); the A. boreas group is taxonomically unsettled, with several former populations now separate species.
fieldMarks: Medium to large stocky toad, 2-5 in (females larger), blunt head, broad waist, short legs, warty skin.
Thin light stripe down the middle of the back from head to rear end.
Prominent oval parotoid glands behind the eyes; no L-shaped cranial crests (Woodhouse's toad has elongate parotoids and L-shaped crests).
Back brown, green, olive, grey or reddish-brown with warts ringed by dark blotches; underside light with irregular dark marks.
Breeding males have smoother skin than females; newly metamorphosed toads lack obvious parotoids and the dorsal stripe may be faint or absent.
behavior: Call is a soft chirruping, plinking peep like a chick, heard day or night and audible only within about 100 ft; a rapid chirp is given as a release call.
Breeds in still or slow water from mid-April at low elevation in western Washington, later at higher elevation; egg strings are laid in shallow water.
Transformed toads are mostly terrestrial but stay near water in drier areas; they dig burrows or use small-mammal burrows, logs or rocks, and overwinter in cold climates.
Feeds on insects and other small invertebrates; at lower elevations active in daylight in cool weather and mostly at night in warm weather.
habitat: Wide range from desert springs to mountain wetlands, using prairies, forests, canyon grasslands and pine-oak habitat.
Breeds in ponds, lakes, reservoir coves, wetlands and river backwaters.
range: Pacific coast from southern Alaska to Baja California and east through the Rocky Mountains to west-central Alberta, Montana, Wyoming, Utah and Colorado; absent from most of the desert Southwest.

lookalikes.name: Woodhouse's toad
lookalikes.howToTell: Woodhouse's toad has L-shaped cranial crests and parotoid glands longer than the eye; the western toad has neither.
